paragraphs.heading: A unit for counting particles
paragraphs.text: The mole, written mol, is the SI unit for amount of substance, one of the system's base units. One mole is exactly 6.02214076×10²³ elementary entities, which may be atoms, molecules, ions, ion pairs or other particles. Written out in full, that is roughly 602 sextillion, or 602 billion times a trillion.

paragraphs.heading: Like a dozen, only vastly bigger
paragraphs.text: A mole works much like the words "pair" or "dozen": each names a group of identical things, not just the number 2 or 12. What makes the mole daunting is that its count is hard to grasp. The reason it is so large is that atoms are tiny. A sample big enough to handle at a lab bench takes not trillions but trillions of trillions of them.

paragraphs.heading: The Avogadro number
paragraphs.text: The count of entities in one mole is called the Avogadro number, N₀, and it is a plain number with no unit. The Avogadro constant, N_A, is that same number given the unit mol⁻¹. Dividing a number of particles N by N_A gives the amount of substance, n = N/N_A, measured in moles. The constant was fixed by counting the ²⁸Si atoms in a single crystal.

paragraphs.heading: How chemists use it
paragraphs.text: Moles give chemists a handy way to state how much of each reactant and product is involved. The equation 2 H₂ + O₂ → 2 H₂O, for instance, can be read as 2 mol of hydrogen and 1 mol of oxygen reacting to make 2 mol of water. A solution's strength is usually given as molar concentration, the amount of dissolved substance in each litre, in mol/L. A substance's molar mass is its relative atomic or molecular mass multiplied by a constant, the molar mass constant, whose value is very close to 1 g/mol.

paragraphs.heading: Equal counts, different stuff
paragraphs.text: Ten moles of water and ten moles of mercury hold the same number of particles, one mercury atom for every water molecule, even though their masses and volumes differ. What counts as one entity depends on the substance. In diamond the whole crystal is in effect a single molecule, so a mole of diamond counts the bonded atoms rather than molecules.

paragraphs.heading: Bigger and smaller moles
paragraphs.text: Chemical engineers rely on the mole too, and for industrial work may scale it up to the kmol of 1000 mol. That switch leaves molarity unchanged, since kmol/m³ = (1000 mol)/(1000 L) = mol/L. Some engineers working in imperial units adopted the pound-mole instead. Growers sometimes rate plant lighting in micromoles of photons per square metre per second. At the small end, one femtomole is exactly 602214076 molecules, while a yoctomole works out to around 0.6 of one molecule.
